text.title: Distribution Channel Research Core Rules
text.summary: Seven rules for scoring and selecting acquisition channels: one CAC definition across all rows, payback period rather than raw CAC as the gate, a single declared time horizon, bounded tests with kill numbers, a concurrency ceiling, and when an imported benchmark may populate a cell.

rule.statement: `scoring` declares one CAC definition applied to all rows: which cost lines are included (media spend, tools, agency fees, content production, loaded SDR/salesperson cost), the attribution model, and the measurement window. Blended CAC and channel-specific paid CAC must never appear in the same column.
rule.rationale: Blended CAC divides total spend across all customers including organic ones, so any row scored blended is arithmetically cheaper than a row scored on its own spend. The ranking then measures where the accounting boundary was drawn rather than which channel acquires efficiently.

rule.statement: Every row carries CAC payback in months = CAC ÷ monthly gross profit per customer, alongside an LTV:CAC ratio. A self-serve or SMB channel with payback beyond ~12 months, or LTV:CAC below 3, fails the gate regardless of how attractive its absolute CAC looks.

rationale.source: David Skok — SaaS Metrics 2.0; Bessemer Venture Partners cloud benchmarks

rule.rationale: CAC in isolation ignores price and gross margin. A cheap channel that sells a low-margin plan is cash-negative for longer than the runway, so winning on it accelerates the funding requirement — the growth is real and the company still fails on cash.

rule.statement: All channels are scored at one stated horizon (e.g. 90 days, or 12 months) and time-to-first-revenue is a separate field, not folded into the score. SEO and content rows must state their compounding lag explicitly rather than showing a first-quarter CAC.

rationale.source: Ahrefs study on time for new pages to reach Google's top 10

rule.rationale: Paid returns a measurable CAC within the same week; organic returns nothing for months and then returns at a near-zero marginal cost. Scoring both inside a 90-day window rejects the channel that would have been cheapest at 18 months, and the rejection is invisible because both cells look populated.

rule.statement: Every entry in `recommended_channels` carries a test definition: fixed budget or time box, one primary metric, the kill threshold committed before spend starts, and the named person who stops it. A recommendation without a kill number is downgraded into `rejected_channels`.

rationale.source: Weinberg & Mares — Traction, Bullseye framework (cheap tests before committing)

rule.rationale: Bullseye's middle ring exists precisely to run cheap tests before scaling. Absent a stop rule the channel is judged on sunk cost and on whoever championed it, so spend continues for months past the point at which the data had already settled.

rule.statement: `recommended_channels` holds no more than 3 entries, exactly one marked primary, each with a named owner. A plan spreading budget evenly across 5 or more channels is rejected outright.

rationale.source: Weinberg & Mares — Traction (concentrate on the one channel that is working)

rule.rationale: Every channel has a competence and volume threshold below which results are statistically indistinguishable from noise. Splitting a small budget puts all of them below it, and the study concludes "nothing works" when what failed was sample size per channel, not the channels.

rule.statement: Any third-party CAC, CPC or conversion benchmark used in `scoring` carries source, year, ACV band, sales motion (self-serve / sales-led) and region. A benchmark from a different ACV band or motion is recorded as context only and MUST NOT populate a scoring cell.

rationale.source: OpenView SaaS Benchmarks — CAC segmented by ACV band and motion

rule.rationale: CAC scales with deal size and with the motion required to close it. Importing an enterprise benchmark into a $30/month self-serve product understates required spend by roughly an order of magnitude, so the plan is under-funded from the first month and the channel is declared dead before it was ever properly funded.

rule.statement: Emit a structured skip when: the product has no paying customers from any source, so no conversion rate exists to score channels against; the total test budget cannot fund even one channel above its noise floor; or one channel already shows channel-market fit and is growing — in which case the question is scaling that channel, not researching new ones.
rule.rationale: Channel research divides a known conversion economics by channel cost. With the numerator unmeasured, every CAC and LTV-fit cell is an assumption, and the ranking reproduces the author's prior with a scoring table wrapped around it.
